options: The range of colors visible to the human eye only
The entire range of electromagnetic radiation, at all wavelengths
A type of sensor used exclusively on drones
The area a single pixel covers on the ground
explain: The electromagnetic spectrum is the entire range of electromagnetic radiation, of which visible light is only a small portion.

q: What is a 'band' in the context of plant science sensing?
options: A physical strap that holds the sensor to the drone
A type of drone propeller
A specific range of wavelengths within the electromagnetic spectrum
The frame rate of a video sensor
explain: A band is a portion of the electromagnetic spectrum — a specific range of wavelengths — used to determine plant health or detect early stress symptoms.

q: Which of these is an example of an active sensor?
options: RGB camera
Thermal camera
LiDAR sensor
Multispectral camera
explain: LiDAR is an active sensor — it emits its own laser wavelength and then detects that same wavelength reflecting back.

q: Why are RGB, multispectral, hyperspectral, and thermal cameras considered passive sensors?
options: They require no battery power
They can only be used at night
They don't collect any data
They detect wavelengths from a source other than themselves, like sunlight
explain: Passive sensors detect wavelengths originating from an external source (like the sun) rather than emitting their own.

q: What's the main difference between a multispectral and a hyperspectral camera?
options: Hyperspectral cameras detect hundreds of narrow bands, while multispectral cameras detect a handful of broader bands
Multispectral cameras only work at night
Multispectral cameras are active sensors and hyperspectral cameras are passive
There is no meaningful difference
explain: Multispectral cameras typically use 6–10 sensors covering broad spectral areas, while hyperspectral cameras capture hundreds of narrow bands, offering much finer spectral detail.

q: What does a thermal camera measure?
options: The amount of visible light reflected from an object
The distance between the sensor and an object
The color of a plant's leaves
Heat reflected or emitted from an object
explain: Unlike RGB, multispectral, or hyperspectral cameras, a thermal camera measures heat rather than reflected light.

q: What does Ground Sampling Distance (GSD) represent?
options: The total area of a field
The speed of the drone during flight
The number of sensors on a drone
The amount of ground area represented by a single pixel
explain: GSD is the amount of ground area covered by one pixel in a captured image — a smaller GSD means finer detail.

q: How does increasing flight altitude affect GSD and spatial resolution?
options: GSD decreases and resolution improves
GSD increases and spatial resolution decreases
Neither GSD nor resolution is affected by altitude
GSD becomes negative
explain: As altitude increases, each pixel covers more ground area, increasing GSD and reducing spatial resolution.

q: What happens to the area covered by each pixel if the focal length is doubled?
options: It doubles
It stays the same
It is cut in half
It becomes zero
explain: A longer focal length narrows the field of view. Doubling the focal length halves the ground area covered by each pixel, increasing spatial resolution.

q: How does increasing image width (more pixels) affect GSD?
options: GSD increases, reducing detail
GSD is unaffected by image width
GSD decreases, increasing detail
Image width has no relationship to GSD
explain: More pixels across the same physical area means each pixel covers less ground, decreasing (improving) the GSD and increasing image detail.
